definition: Repression (Verdrängung/压抑): the fundamental defense mechanism by which representations linked to a drive are kept in or pushed into the unconscious. Freud distinguishes primal repression (Urverdrängung), which creates the initial unconscious nucleus and fixation, from repression proper (eigentliche Verdrängung/Nachdrängen), which pushes derivatives of the primal repressed back into the unconscious. Repression is dynamic, requiring continuous counter-cathexis (Gegenbesetzung) to maintain. The return of the repressed manifests as symptoms, dreams, and parapraxes. Freud called repression 'the corner-stone on which the whole structure of psychoanalysis rests.'
connective_patterns: Verdrängung operates on Trieb representatives, not on the Trieb itself
the return of the repressed (Wiederkehr des Verdrängten) manifests through Verdichtung and Verschiebung in dreams and symptoms

definition: Drive (Trieb/驱力): a constant force (konstante Kraft) originating at the border between the somatic and the psychic, characterized by four components: source (Quelle), pressure (Drang), aim (Ziel), and object (Objekt). Unlike instinct (Instinkt), which has a fixed biological object and aim, the drive has no predetermined object — the object is its most variable element. Strachey's Standard Edition mistranslates Trieb as 'instinct,' obscuring Freud's crucial distinction. The drives are dualistic: Eros (life drives) vs. Todestrieb (death drive) in the final theory, or sexual drives vs. ego drives in the earlier framework.
connective_patterns: Trieb exerts constant pressure unlike stimulus which acts as single impact
Trieb is a Grenzbegriff (limit-concept) between psychic and somatic

definition: The Unconscious (das Unbewusste/无意识): in the descriptive sense, all mental content not currently in consciousness; in the dynamic sense, content actively kept from consciousness by repression; in the systematic/topographical sense (first topography), the system Ucs governed by primary process (free energy, condensation, displacement, timelessness, no negation, no contradiction). The unconscious is constituted through primal repression (Urverdrängung) and populated by repressed representatives and their derivatives. Its contents seek discharge according to the pleasure principle and are known only through their derivatives: dreams, symptoms, parapraxes, and jokes.
connective_patterns: das Unbewusste is structured by primary process — Verdichtung and Verschiebung
the contents of das Unbewusste are known only through Traumdeutung, symptoms, and parapraxes

definition: Transference (Übertragung/移情): the process by which unconscious wishes, feelings, and relational patterns originally directed toward early significant figures (especially parents) are displaced onto the person of the analyst. Initially regarded by Freud as pure resistance (Widerstand) impeding recall of repressed memories, transference was later recognized as both obstacle and vehicle of treatment — the 'playground' where the patient's conflicts are enacted in vivo. Freud distinguished positive transference (affectionate feelings facilitating treatment) from negative transference (hostile feelings opposing treatment) and erotic transference.
connective_patterns: Übertragung is the clinical manifestation of Wiederholungszwang — the patient acts out rather than remembers
Übertragung and Widerstand are the two fundamental facts of psychoanalytic treatment

definition: Resistance (Widerstand/阻抗): the patient's unconscious opposition to the analytic process, manifesting as all forces within the patient that oppose the procedures and processes of psychoanalytic work. Freud identified five types: repression resistance (from the ego), transference resistance (from the ego), secondary gain resistance (from the ego), id resistance (compulsion to repeat), and superego resistance (unconscious guilt, need for punishment). Resistance is not an obstacle to be eliminated but a clinical phenomenon to be analyzed — 'the process of bringing unconscious material to light is performed in the face of continuous resistance.'
connective_patterns: Widerstand and Übertragung are the two observed facts that psychoanalytic theory attempts to account for
Widerstand operates through all mechanisms of Abwehr (defense)

definition: The Ego (das Ich/自我, literally 'the I'): in the structural model (1923), the agency mediating between the demands of the id (Es), the superego (Über-Ich), and external reality. Operating under the reality principle, the ego deploys defense mechanisms (Abwehrmechanismen), manages perception, motility, memory, and reality-testing. Freud describes the ego as 'a poor creature owing service to three masters' — the id, the superego, and the external world. The ego is not master in its own house: it is partly unconscious, and its defensive operations (repression, etc.) are themselves unconscious. Strachey's Latinized 'ego' obscures Freud's deliberate use of the everyday German 'Ich.'
connective_patterns: das Ich mediates between Es, Über-Ich, and external reality
das Ich deploys Verdrängung and other Abwehrmechanismen against Trieb demands

definition: The Id (das Es/本我, literally 'the It'): in the structural model (1923), the oldest psychical agency, entirely unconscious, containing the innate drives (Triebe) and everything repressed. The Es operates according to the pleasure principle via primary process, tolerating no delay in satisfaction and knowing neither negation, contradiction, nor time. Freud described it as 'the dark, inaccessible part of our personality' — a 'cauldron full of seething excitations' (ein Kessel voll brodelnder Erregungen). The term was borrowed from Georg Groddeck, who in turn took it from Nietzsche. The id has no organization, produces no collective will, and follows only the pleasure principle.
connective_patterns: das Es is the reservoir of Trieb energy (libido)
das Es seeks immediate discharge according to the Lustprinzip via primary process

definition: The Superego (das Über-Ich/超我, literally 'the Over-I'): in the structural model (1923), the psychical agency that functions as conscience, self-observation, and carrier of the ego ideal (Ichideal). Formed through internalization of parental prohibitions and cultural norms during the resolution of the Oedipus complex, the superego inherits the severity of the father's prohibition rather than the actual father's behavior. It operates partly unconsciously, generating guilt, need for punishment, and moral anxiety. The superego can be excessively harsh — 'the superego can be super-moral and then become as cruel as only the id can be.'
connective_patterns: das Über-Ich is the heir of the Ödipuskomplex
das Über-Ich generates moral Angst as counterpart to realistic anxiety and neurotic anxiety

definition: Dream-interpretation (Traumdeutung/释梦): Freud's method and theory of deciphering dreams as 'the royal road to a knowledge of the unconscious activities of the mind.' All dreams are wish-fulfillments (Wunscherfüllung): the dream-work (Traumarbeit) transforms latent dream-thoughts into the manifest dream through four operations — condensation (Verdichtung), displacement (Verschiebung), considerations of representability (Rücksicht auf Darstellbarkeit), and secondary revision (sekundäre Bearbeitung). The latent content contains the repressed wish; the manifest content is the disguised, censored product. Published in 1899/1900, Die Traumdeutung established the psychoanalytic method.
connective_patterns: Traumdeutung reveals the operations of Verdichtung and Verschiebung as primary process mechanisms
the Traumarbeit transforms latent content via the same mechanisms governing symptom formation

definition: The Pleasure Principle (Lustprinzip/快感原则): the regulatory principle governing the primary process, according to which mental activity aims at avoiding unpleasure (Unlust) and obtaining pleasure (Lust) through the most immediate discharge of excitation. The German Lust carries a dual meaning — both pleasure and desire. The pleasure principle governs the id (Es) and the unconscious system. It is modified but not abolished by the reality principle (Realitätsprinzip), which defers immediate satisfaction for more certain future satisfaction. The pleasure-unpleasure principle was Freud's earliest metapsychological principle, operative already in the 1895 Project for a Scientific Psychology.
connective_patterns: the Lustprinzip governs the Es and primary process
the Wiederholungszwang operates jenseits des Lustprinzips (beyond the pleasure principle)

definition: Repetition Compulsion (Wiederholungszwang/强迫重复): the tendency to repeat repressed experiences rather than remember them, operating beyond the pleasure principle. First defined in 'Remembering, Repeating and Working-Through' (1914): 'the patient does not remember anything of what he has forgotten and repressed, he acts it out.' In Beyond the Pleasure Principle (1920), Freud elevated this clinical observation to a metapsychological principle — repetition compulsion is 'more primitive, more elementary, more instinctual than the pleasure principle which it overrides,' rooted in the drive's inherent tendency to restore an earlier state (the inorganic). The concept bridges clinical observation (transference repetition) and speculative metapsychology (death drive).
connective_patterns: Wiederholungszwang manifests clinically as Übertragung — the patient repeats instead of remembers
Wiederholungszwang led Freud to postulate the Todestrieb as operating beyond the Lustprinzip

definition: The Death Drive (Todestrieb/死驱力): postulated in Beyond the Pleasure Principle (1920), the drive toward dissolution, the return to the inorganic state — 'the aim of all life is death.' Opposed to Eros (life drives), the death drive manifests as aggression, destructiveness, and the compulsion to repeat. Freud grounded it in the conservative nature of drives: 'an instinct is an urge inherent in organic life to restore an earlier state of things.' The death drive is silent (stumm) and works internally (primary masochism) before being deflected outward as aggression. The term Thanatos was introduced by Stekel, not Freud. Freud acknowledged the concept met 'resistance even in analytic circles.'
connective_patterns: Todestrieb manifests through Wiederholungszwang beyond the Lustprinzip
Todestrieb is initially directed inward (primary masochism) before deflection outward as Aggression

definition: Cathexis (Besetzung/贯注, literally 'occupation'): the investment or charging of psychic energy (libido) in a mental representation, object, or psychical structure. Freud used military metaphors: psychic energy 'occupies' (besetzt) mental territory as troops occupy positions. Strachey coined the Latinized 'cathexis' in 1922 despite Freud's reservations about its technicality. Key distinctions: object-cathexis (Objektbesetzung) vs. ego-cathexis (Ichbesetzung/narcissistic libido); cathexis (Besetzung) vs. counter-cathexis (Gegenbesetzung) sustaining repression; and hypercathexis (Überbesetzung) involved in attention and preconscious processing. Dream-work redistributes cathexis from important latent thoughts to indifferent manifest elements.
connective_patterns: Besetzung is the economic dimension of metapsychology alongside topographic and dynamic dimensions
Verdrängung requires continuous Gegenbesetzung to maintain the repressed in the unconscious

definition: Condensation (Verdichtung/凝缩): one of the two principal mechanisms of dream-work (Traumarbeit), by which multiple latent dream-thoughts are compressed into a single manifest element. A single dream-image may be a composite of several persons, places, or ideas (overdetermination/Überdeterminierung), explaining why manifest dreams are far more concise than the latent thoughts behind them. Condensation also operates in symptom formation, jokes (Witz), and parapraxes (Fehlleistungen). Lacan equated condensation with the rhetorical figure of metaphor, as displacement corresponds to metonymy. Condensation is a primary process operation — the preferred mode of functioning of the unconscious id.
connective_patterns: Verdichtung and Verschiebung are the two principal Traumarbeit mechanisms
Verdichtung produces overdetermined (überdeterminiert) composite formations in dreams and symptoms

definition: Displacement (Verschiebung/移置, literally 'shift'): one of the two principal mechanisms of dream-work, by which psychic emphasis (interest, affect, intensity) is shifted from an important latent element to an indifferent or peripheral manifest element. Verschiebung serves the dream-censorship by disguising the latent content, and serves psychic economy by allowing affect-charges to transfer freely between representations. Beyond dreams, displacement operates in symptom formation, phobias (displacement of anxiety onto substitute objects), and jokes. Lacan linked displacement to the trope of metonymy, as condensation corresponds to metaphor. Displacement is a primary process operation following the pleasure principle.
connective_patterns: Verschiebung shifts affect from significant latent thoughts to indifferent manifest elements
Verschiebung and Verdichtung together constitute the primary process operations of the Unbewusste

definition: Deferred Action / Afterwardsness (Nachträglichkeit/追溯性): Freud's concept of retroactive temporality, whereby an earlier experience (typically sexual) acquires traumatic significance only when a later experience retroactively activates and reinterprets it. Conceived in the Project for a Scientific Psychology (1895): trauma is constituted through two etiological moments — the initial event and its subsequent reactivation. Nachträglichkeit challenges linear causality: the past is restructured from the present, not merely recalled. The concept was revived by Lacan (1953) and has been translated variously as 'deferred action' (Strachey), 'après-coup' (French), and 'afterwardsness' (Thomä and Cheshire), each capturing only one vector of its bidirectional temporality.
connective_patterns: Nachträglichkeit restructures the past retroactively — the second scene gives the first scene its traumatic valence
Nachträglichkeit implies that Verdrängung is not a single event but a temporal process requiring two moments

definition: Anxiety (Angst/焦虑): an affective state of unpleasure accompanied by motor discharge and perception of that discharge. Freud's theory underwent two major phases: (1) First theory (pre-1926): anxiety results from the automatic transformation of undischarged libido — repression causes anxiety. (2) Second theory (Inhibitions, Symptoms and Anxiety, 1926): anxiety is a signal (Signalangst) produced by the ego to mobilize defenses — anxiety causes repression. Three types: realistic anxiety (Realangst, response to external danger), neurotic anxiety (from the id's demands), and moral anxiety (from the superego's prohibitions/guilt). Castration anxiety (Kastrationsangst) is central to the Oedipus complex and drives its resolution. Birth anxiety (Geburtsangst) is the prototype of all later anxiety states.
connective_patterns: Angst as signal triggers Verdrängung and other defense mechanisms in the second anxiety theory
Kastrationsangst drives resolution of the Ödipuskomplex and formation of the Über-Ich

definition: The Oedipus Complex (Ödipuskomplex/俄狄浦斯情结): the structured set of loving and hostile wishes the child experiences toward the parents during the phallic phase (ages 3-5). In its positive form: desire for the opposite-sex parent and rivalry with the same-sex parent. In its negative (inverted) form: desire for the same-sex parent and rivalry with the opposite-sex parent. The complete Oedipus complex combines both forms. Its dissolution through castration anxiety (boys) or penis envy (girls) leads to identification with the same-sex parent and formation of the superego (Über-Ich). Freud considered the Oedipus complex 'the nuclear complex of the neuroses' and its resolution 'the most important social achievement of the human mind.'
connective_patterns: resolution of the Ödipuskomplex through Kastrationsangst produces the Über-Ich as its heir
the Ödipuskomplex is the nuclear complex (Kernkomplex) of all neuroses

definition: Narcissism (Narzissmus/自恋): the libidinal investment of the ego (Ichbesetzung) as distinguished from object-cathexis (Objektbesetzung). Freud's 'On Narcissism' (1914) distinguishes: primary narcissism (primärer Narzissmus), the original libidinal cathexis of the ego in infancy before object-cathexis; and secondary narcissism (sekundärer Narzissmus), the withdrawal of libido from external objects back to the ego (as in psychosis, mourning, sleep). Narcissism revealed that ego-libido and object-libido exist in an inverse economic relationship — the more libido is invested in external objects, the less remains for the ego, and vice versa. The essay also introduced the ego ideal (Ichideal), later developed into the superego concept.
connective_patterns: Narzissmus established the inverse economic relation between Ichbesetzung and Objektbesetzung
primary Narzissmus is the developmental precursor of the Ichideal and later the Über-Ich

definition: Sublimation (Sublimierung/升华): the process by which the sexual drive (Sexualtrieb) is deflected toward a new, non-sexual aim of higher social or cultural valuation — artistic creation, intellectual inquiry, professional achievement. Unlike repression, sublimation allows the drive partial satisfaction through a socially acceptable substitute, making it the most 'successful' defense mechanism and the basis of civilization's cultural achievements. Sublimation passes through narcissistic libido: 'the ego changes sexual object-libido into narcissistic libido, and then gives it a different aim.' Freud never fully elaborated the mechanism of sublimation, acknowledging it remained one of the least understood concepts in psychoanalysis.
connective_patterns: Sublimierung channels Trieb energy into culturally valued activity without Verdrängung
Sublimierung passes through Narzissmus — object-libido is first narcissized then redirected to a non-sexual aim
